chapter: The Second Herd and its sidemen
title: Harris and his trombone section buddies
summary: Harris would demand better trombonists, then relent because they were his friends, and made them play far above themselves.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: He certainly gave the band -- among others, but I'm particularly thinking about him -- a very distinctive sound because of his solos.
And he did something which I think was truly remarkable. I'd never witnessed this anywhere, ever, before or since. He took two very competent trombonists, but
really with no feeling for jazz particularly, or -- they could play the trombone, let's leave it that way, and it doesn't matter who they were because that's not the import of this.

But at least once every couple of weeks, Bill would come to me and say, "Man, we got to get some trombone players. We ain't making it. These guys are driving me crazy." So I'd give him the same stock answer. "Bill, who do you want? Just give me their names, we'll call them, we'll hire them, all right?"
An hour later he'd come back to me and say, "Oh, man, forget what I said. We can't -- those are good guys." Are you ready for this? It was the fact that they were his bosom buddies.

From day to day, week to week. And the amazing thing out of all of it is the fact that he'd had these guys playing so far above their heads, from what they could normally do, that it was unbelievable. They sounded like -- three guys sounded like a five-trombone section.
Was he like this even through the late '50s, when he came back and did another --
